item.title: Recent developments in spatial econometrics
item.description: arXiv:2611.14673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We conduct a non-exhaustive survey of the recent spatial econometrics literature by placing it in historical context and mapping current trends. The focus will be primarily on methodological aspects. Starting from the canonical spatial autoregressive model, we cover its many extensions and richer parameterizations. We discuss spatial panel data models and advancements in the study of nonlinear and nonparametric models. Specification testing for spatial econometric models, with its roots in the $J$-test of Davidson and MacKinnon (1981), is also covered, as is spatial correlation robust inference. Finally, we review advancements in general limit theory, limited dependent variable models, spatial weight matrix estimation and endogeneity, recent attempts at uniting the network formation and spatial literature, and sundry important topics. We take stock of the current paradigm and critically evaluate the impact of the spatial literature on applied practice.
item.dc:creator: Abhimanyu Gupta

item.title: Identification of Rational Inattention-Additive Random Utility Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.14752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a novel class of econometric models, called Rational Inattention-Additive Random Utility Models. It is based on the discrete choice rational inattention model of Matvejka and McKay (2015) with additive unobserved heterogeneity incorporated. We show that some of the systematic components of the primitives of the model are nonparametrically identified even if the distributions of unobserved variables and the prior of decision makers are both unknown to the Econometrician. If additional information about the prior is known to the Econometrician, even stronger identification results become available.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Kristensen, Ruolei Zhu

item.title: Lost in the Bins: Treatment Effects with Discretized Covariates
item.description: arXiv:2611.14789v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mean independence restrictions are widely used to identify average treatment effects, but the covariates used to formulate these restrictions are often observed or used in coarsened form. This paper shows that mean independence conditional on a finely measured covariate need not hold after the covariate is replaced by a coarsened version. Coarsening can therefore change the identifying content of the comparison rather than only the precision of estimation. I characterize the resulting coarsening bias for the ATT and ATE. For the ATT, the bias is driven by within-cell composition in untreated potential outcomes. For the ATE, an additional treatment effect heterogeneity term appears. I then introduce $c$-mean dependence, a nonparametric relaxation of exact mean independence at the coarsened level, and derive sharp bounds for average treatment effects. The parameter $c$ determines how far comparisons may extend across neighboring values of the coarsened covariate. I propose sample analogue estimators and bootstrap inference procedures for the resulting bound functions. In an application to voluntary military service using data from Angrist (1998), positive effects on early earnings, which primarily reflect military pay, hold even under the weakest form of $c$-mean dependence, whereas the evidence on later effects on civilian earnings is inconclusive once mean independence is relaxed.
item.dc:creator: Cenchen Liu

item.title: Inference After Model Refutation: Uniform Post-Relaxation Inference for Partially Identified Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.15552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When data reject an econometric model, the researcher must decide which identifying assumptions to give up. If several equally preferred repairs restore compatibility, the repair itself is unknown, and inference under any one of them can exclude structural values supported by the others, even when that inference is exact. I propose Post-Relaxation Projection (PR), which carries one simultaneous confidence event through every repair that may be minimal. With repair-by-repair primitive bounds, PR equals the union of all post-relaxation targets compatible with the band, so no smaller band-based set has the same guarantee. I derive limits on learning the repair, the exact perturbation radius of the minimal-repair correspondence, oracle-equivalent adaptation, and a reduced-form version valid at zero first stages. In cross-country data on institutions and income, the data do not settle which historical instrument should be dropped, yet every admissible minimum repair implies a positive effect of institutions.
item.dc:creator: Ulrich Hounyo

item.title: Introducing and Repealing an EV Subsidy: Evidence from New Zealand's Clean Car Discount
item.description: arXiv:2611.15947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: New Zealand's Clean Car Discount (CCD) was a feebate scheme that offered rebates for low-emission vehicles from July 2021, added fees for high-emission vehicles from April 2022, and was abolished at the end of December 2023. Shortly afterwards, road user charges were introduced for electric vehicles (EVs). We study how EV adoption responded to the introduction and the abrupt repeal of the scheme, using monthly vehicle registration data from 2014 to 2024. A structural break analysis following Bai and Perron, combined with a regression discontinuity in time, shows that breaks in the registrations of battery electric, plug-in hybrid and conventional vehicles coincide with the policy dates. To estimate causal effects, we apply a difference-in-differences approach with Queensland, Australia, as a comparison region and Newey-West standard errors. Because the New Zealand market was about four times larger, the analysis uses log-transformed registrations, so that parallel trends refer to equal growth rates. The results are asymmetric. After the introduction of the rebates, EV registrations in New Zealand rose strongly, but by a similar proportion as in Queensland, and the average effect relative to Queensland is not statistically significant. A specification allowing for a change in slope suggests a gradual acceleration of EV uptake. After the repeal, EV registrations fell by about 72% relative to Queensland, and the decline persisted in 2025. Both policy dates were preceded by a rush of purchases. The average CO2 emissions of newly registered vehicles fell markedly during the scheme and rebounded after its end. The results suggest that an abrupt end of EV purchase incentives can cause a large and lasting drop in EV uptake, and that a gradual, pre-announced phase-out may be preferable.
item.dc:creator: Fabian Dunker, Jyotsna Garg

item.title: Testing Density Discontinuity Using Spacings
item.description: arXiv:2611.16199v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the regression discontinuity design, researchers assess the credibility of assumptions by testing the running variable's density for a discontinuity at the cutoff. This paper proposes a novel such test. The test uses q spacings on each side of the cutoff, where spacings are the widths between ordered observations. Spacings yield a continuous statistic that behaves well under weak assumptions. I study its properties in two asymptotic frameworks: one where q is fixed as the sample size increases and one where q slowly diverges to infinity. With q fixed, the test achieves exact asymptotic size control without user randomization. When q increases slowly, the test becomes consistent without sacrificing exact asymptotic size. Compared to the preferred version of Bugni and Canay's (2021) test, the only other test with comparably weak assumptions, this test reduces sensitivity to the tuning parameter and performs similarly when theirs is well-chosen.
item.dc:creator: William T. Firmin

item.title: Uniform Inference for Two-Way Clustered Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.16584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish uniformly asymptotically exact inference for the population mean of two-way clustered data, allowing the data-generating process to vary with sample size. This finding does not contradict the well-known impossibility result of Menzel (2021), which places a fundamental limit on uniform estimation of the asymptotic distribution of the normalized full-array mean. We estimate the same population mean by averaging the sample means from random matchings. A closed-form standard error makes the resulting confidence interval straightforward to implement. The variance estimator is positive semidefinite and the studentized matching estimator is uniformly asymptotically standard normal. The cost of uniform validity is a slower convergence rate under degeneracy. We extend the result to smooth functions of GMM parameters, allowing the different moment components to exhibit different dependence regimes. In simulations, the proposed confidence intervals achieve coverage close to the nominal level across the dependence regimes considered.
item.dc:creator: Ulrich Hounyo, Jiahao Lin, Xiaojun Song, Hansheng Wang

item.title: A Sensitivity Framework for Assessing External Validity
item.description: arXiv:2611.16242v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Assessing the external validity of experimental results is a pervasive challenge in causal inference as internally valid findings need not generalize beyond sites in which the experiments were conducted. Since the number of sites is often smaller than the number of site-level variables that moderate causal effects, we develop a partial identification framework that lets practitioners assess external validity under a wide range of assumptions that allow extrapolation across site-level variables. Our optimization-driven approach can accommodate any affine family of parameter restrictions, such as interaction terms being dominated by direct effects (the "effect hierarchy principle"). Since standard estimating-equation arguments do not apply in our setting---underspecified parameter directions responsible for partial identification make the covariance matrix singular---we develop a novel debiasing approach for estimands given by constrained optimization problems, giving rise to semiparametrically efficient estimators for our flexible partial identification bounds. We illustrate our approach on multi-site microcredit experiments harmonized by Meager (2019), whose lending environments differ widely in interest rates, loan sizes, and promotion. Holding out one country at a time, we construct external-validity intervals for the held-out country from the remaining source sites and show how our framework connects different extrapolation assumptions to concrete partial identification bounds.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Boyarsky, Naoki Egami, Hongseok Namkoong

item.title: One-Sided Randomization in Two-Sided Platform Experiments: Which Side Should be Randomized?
item.description: arXiv:2611.16406v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Two-sided marketplace platforms often use randomized experiments to evaluate new features, raising the question of whether to randomize customers or listings. Randomizing the smaller (\emph{short}) side can reduce interference bias due to weaker competition, while randomizing the larger (\emph{long}) side provides a larger nominal sample, potentially reducing variance. On the surface, these competing considerations suggest a bias-variance trade-off in choosing which side to randomize. We investigate this trade-off in a two-sided marketplace with first-come, first-served (FCFS) booking and heterogeneous customer preferences, studying the bias and variance of difference-in-means estimators of the global average treatment effect. Our findings suggest that rather than a bias-variance tradeoff, in fact short-side randomization is generally preferable on {\em both} dimensions. We prove these results in an asymptotic regime where market imbalance increases. We establish conditions under which (1) short-side randomization eliminates first-order interference bias, while long-side randomization retains it; and (2) short-side randomization also achieves a variance rate of no larger asymptotic order than long-side randomization. The key insight is that although the long side contains more participants, the number of matches is constrained by the population on the short side, limiting the apparent variance advantage of randomizing a larger sample. Our conditions accommodate heterogeneous preferences and treatment effects and are satisfied by familiar logit models of customer choice. Together, these findings support randomizing on the short side, despite the larger sample size available on the long side.
item.dc:creator: Ramesh Johari, Anushka Murthy

item.title: Localizing Mean Shifts in High-Dimensional Vector Autoregressive Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.16556v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the localization of mean changes in high-dimensional vector autoregressions (VARs) when the autoregressive dynamics remain common across regimes. We develop a three-step procedure that first obtains preliminary change-point estimates from the raw series ignoring the dependence structure, then estimates a common sparse VAR using observations away from the estimated changes, and finally filters the series to refine the change point locations. For a single change point, we show that the preliminary localization rate depends directly on the strength of temporal dependence, whereas filtering removes this dependence penalty from the oracle rate. With an estimated filter, the refined rate additionally reflects the error in estimating the VAR dynamics and the relation between the change in the stationary mean and the corresponding change in the VAR intercept. We characterize these rates explicitly and establish conditions under which filtering improves localization. Because filtering near a change point uses lags from adjacent regimes, it also creates a short-lived distortion in the filtered mean; we characterize when this boundary effect is innocuous and develop a transition-corrected alternative. We extend the procedure to an unknown number of change points. Overlapping local windows are used to generate candidate locations, an information criterion removes redundant and spurious candidates and estimates the number of changes, and the retained locations are subsequently refined using the estimated VAR filter. We establish consistency for the estimated number of changes and simultaneous localization rates for their locations. Numerical experiments corroborate the localization gains and show robustness to moderate departures from common VAR dynamics. An application to a large panel of U.S. macroeconomic indicators identifies economically interpretable changes.
item.dc:creator: Hongqiang Sun, Sayar Karmakar, George Michailidis

item.title: Finite Sample Inference in Incomplete Models
item.description: arXiv:2204.00473v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose confidence regions for the parameters of incomplete models with exact coverage of the true parameter in finite samples. Our confidence region inverts a test, which generalizes Monte Carlo tests to incomplete models. The test statistic is a discrete analogue of a new optimal-transport formulation of the structural model. Both test statistic and critical values rely on simulation draws from the distribution of latent variables and are computed using solutions to discrete optimal transport, hence linear programming problems. We also propose a fast preliminary search in the parameter space with an alternative, more conservative yet consistent test, based on a parameter-free critical value. We show that this test is maximally consistent in the following sense: under infinite exchangeability, it consistently rejects every data-generating process that some test with finite-sample size control consistently rejects. We compare size and power of our procedure with competing proposals in simulations based on a regression with interval valued regressors. A second simulation based on latent consideration sets shows that dependent selection can severely distort inference calibrated under i.i.d. sampling, while our procedure retains finite-sample size control. Finally, we apply our methodology to the model of airline entry and price competition in Ciliberto et al. [2021].
item.dc:creator: Lixiong Li, Marc Henry

item.title: Inference for High-Dimensional Regression with a Possible Threshold
item.description: arXiv:2404.08105v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops uniform inference for slope coefficients in high-dimensional threshold regressions without pretesting for a threshold effect. Confidence intervals based on a debiased threshold Lasso estimator are uniformly asymptotically valid, allowing for heteroskedasticity and non-sub-Gaussian covariates and errors. We also propose a threshold-effect test and extend inference to stationary time series. Applying the method to racial tipping in U.S. neighborhoods, we find that the relationships between white population change and residential turnover, housing age, commuting schedules, and utility payments differ across minority-share regimes. Threshold effects are detected in fewer metropolitan areas in 2000--2010 than in 1990--2000.
item.dc:creator: Jiatong Li, Hongqiang Yan

item.title: Prediction Sets and Conformal Inference with Interval Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2501.10117v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Given data on a random variable $Y$, a prediction set with miscoverage level $\alpha \in (0,1)$ is a set that contains a new draw of $Y$ with probability at least $1-\alpha$. Among all prediction sets satisfying this coverage property, the oracle prediction set is the one with minimal volume. The oracle prediction set offers a complementary view of the distribution of $Y$, beyond point estimators such as the mean and quantiles, and has attracted considerable interest recently. This paper develops methods for estimating such prediction sets conditional on observed covariates when $Y$ censored or interval-valued. We characterise the oracle prediction set under partial identification induced by interval censoring and propose consistent estimators for both oracle prediction intervals and more general oracle prediction sets consisting of multiple disjoint intervals. In addition, we apply conformal inference to construct finite-sample valid prediction sets for interval outcomes that remain consistent as the sample size grows, using a conformity score tailored to interval data. The proposed procedure accounts for irreducible prediction uncertainty due to the stochastic nature of outcomes, modelling uncertainty arising from partial identification, and sampling uncertainty that vanishes as sample size increases. We conduct Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical applications using UK job postings data and the US Current Population Survey. The results demonstrate the robustness and efficiency of the proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Weiguang Liu, \'Aureo de Paula, Elie Tamer

item.title: When is p-hacking detectable?
item.description: arXiv:2506.20035v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that some forms of p-hacking and publication bias cannot be detected by examining the histogram of t-statistics or their p-values. Even when p-hacking is detectable, standard tests may lack power against some alternatives. We propose a novel test that is consistent against every form of selective reporting that is detectable from the distribution of reported t-statistics. Our test statistic is the distance between the smoothed empirical t-curve and the set of possible honest distributions. Unlike existing tests which target roughness or incorrect derivatives in the t-curve and p-curve, the projection test is much less sensitive to rounding and derounding of the printed t-scores and we provide a novel deterministic derounding procedure that preserves its validity. In an empirical application to economics articles we show that the projection test rejects more often than any of seven tests from Elliott et al. (2022) and Simonsohn et al. (2014, 2015). Moreover, the projection test certifies that detection was not driven by rounding or derounding. In a simulation exercise that resamples actual medical trials we show that there are simple p-hacking techniques that the projection test detects but the others do not.
item.dc:creator: Stefan Faridani

item.title: Improving control over unobservables with network data
item.description: arXiv:2511.00612v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a method to conduct causal inference in the presence of unobserved confounders by leveraging networks with homophily, a frequently observed tendency to form edges with similar nodes. I introduce a concept of asymptotic homophily, according to which individuals' selectivity scales with the size of the potential connection pool. The resulting network formation model accommodates common empirical features such as homophily, degree heterogeneity, sparsity, and clustering, and provides a framework to obtain consistent estimators of treatment effects that are robust to selection on unobservables. In an application, I recover an estimate of the effect of parental involvement on students' test scores that is greater than that of OLS, arguably due to the estimator's ability to account for unobserved ability.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Starck

item.title: Empirical Bayes Estimation in Heterogeneous Coefficient Panel Models
item.description: arXiv:2601.07059v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop an empirical Bayes (EB) G-modeling framework for short-panel linear models with nonparametric prior for the random intercepts, slopes, dynamics, and non-spherical error variances. We establish identification and consistency of the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) under general conditions, and provide low-level sufficient conditions for several models of empirical interest. Conditions for regret consistency of the EB estimators are also established. The NPMLE is computed using a Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao gradient flow algorithm adapted to panel regressions. Using data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, we find that the slope coefficient for potential experience is substantially heterogeneous and negatively correlated with the random intercept, and that error variances and autoregressive coefficients vary considerably across individuals. The EB estimates reduce mean squared prediction errors relative to individual maximum likelihood estimates.
item.dc:creator: Myunghyun Song, Sokbae Lee, Serena Ng

item.title: Maximum score and non-smooth M-estimators with multiway dependence
item.description: arXiv:2604.10232v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Under i.i.d. sampling, the maximum score estimator of Manski (1975) converges at the cube-root rate to a non-Gaussian limit, and under median independence alone no regular estimator attains the parametric rate Chamberlain (1986). We show that, under multiway dependence and low-level conditions, the estimator is asymptotically normal at a parametric rate in the smallest number of clusters and, when the cluster-level variance is non-degenerate, as fast as regular estimators such as probit. The result rests on a general theory for non-smooth M-estimators, under which a modified bootstrap is first-order valid given a consistent Hessian estimate. With two-way clustering a cube-root term can remain. We then develop two-scale non-standard asymptotics, in which the limit is a Gaussian vector plus an independent Chernoff-type vector and either term may dominate, along sequences of laws from a non-degenerate cluster-level variance to the degenerate case. Under high-level conditions, the symmetric bootstrap intervals for suitable scalar parameters control size uniformly over such classes of laws, asymptotically exactly where the Gaussian term dominates and conservatively otherwise.
item.dc:creator: Harold D. Chiang, Ahnaf Rafi

item.title: A Practical Guide to Instrumental Variables Methods with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
item.description: arXiv:2605.15115v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Instrumental variables (IV) methods are central to applied microeconomics. While classical approaches assume linear models with constant effects, recent literature has shifted toward the local average treatment effect (LATE) framework to accommodate heterogeneous treatment effects. This paper provides a practical guide to aligning empirical practice with recent theory. We first examine how different specifications with covariates lead to distinct weighted averages of covariate-specific LATEs. We then discuss how parametric misspecification can undermine the causal interpretation of these estimands and suggest flexible specifications as essential robustness checks. Finally, we review formal tests for LATE assumptions and methods robust to monotonicity violations. We provide a guide to software implementations to help researchers apply the methods in practice.
item.dc:creator: Tymon S{\l}oczy\'nski, Liyang Sun, S. Derya Uysal

item.title: Quantile restrictions, revealed rankings, and the limits of multinomial choice
item.description: arXiv:2608.16708v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper analyzes when choice probabilities reveal rankings of deterministic utility indices in semiparametric discrete choice models. It begins with binary choice, showing that quantile thresholds can arise from behavioral departures from utility maximization under exchangeable unobservables, or from non-exchangeable unobservables under utility maximization. These behavioral and distributional routes are then extended to multinomial choice. Under limited attention, balance restrictions on attention probabilities give linear separators whose strict signs reveal rankings uniformly over admissible unobservable distributions and parameter values. Beyond these restrictions, opposite rankings can generate overlapping probability images. Under non-exchangeable unobservables, a common ranking partition across distributions need not exist. Under a common location-scale structure, both extensions admit an injective, generally nonlinear probability map that permits ranking recovery on its attainable image. The results distinguish distribution-robust ranking rules from recovery under specific structural restrictions, clarifying the limits of extending binary quantile restrictions to multinomial choice.
item.dc:creator: Tatiana Komarova

item.title: Tractable Estimation of the Money Pump Index
item.description: arXiv:2609.16086v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Money Pump Index (MPI) of Echenique et al. (2011) measures the severity of consumer irrationality, but computing the exact mean and median MPI over all revealed preference cycles is NP-hard (Smeulders et al., 2013). Existing solutions rely on heuristic proxies, such as evaluating only shorter cycles or bounding the MPI. By framing revealed preferences as a directed graph, this paper projects choice violations onto fundamental cycle bases, which are minimal sets of linearly independent cycles that span the graph's entire cycle space. This yields computationally tractable estimators for the mean and median MPI that are asymptotically equivalent to the original MPI. Applying this methodology to the scanner dataset analyzed by Echenique et al. (2011) and Smeulders et al., (2013), the proposed estimators compute quickly and with negligible small-sample bias.
item.dc:creator: Gavin Kader

item.title: Bayesian Machine Learning Methods For Large Scale Demand Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.08409v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work studies how Bayesian machine learning methods can be used for large-scale demand estimation with many product categories. I compare two model classes, a latent factorization model and a mixed logit model and two Bayesian estimation approaches, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and Variational Inference (VI). The analysis combines a simulation study with an application to supermarket scanner data. The results show that the latent factorization model benefits from information across categories and improves its predictive performance as the dimensionality of the choice environment increases, whereas the mixed logit model does not exhibit the same pattern. MCMC delivers the highest predictive accuracy but is computationally intensive. VI achieves slightly lower predictive performance while substantially reducing runtime. In the empirical application, VI also outperforms the mixed logit benchmark. These findings highlight a trade-off between accuracy and computational feasibility in multi-category demand estimation.
item.dc:creator: Anna B. Schmidt

item.title: Doubly robust estimation of direct and spillover effects using multiple pre-treatment periods
item.description: arXiv:2610.37049v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. Under certain identifying assumptions, both components may be identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, even in the absence of an uncontaminated comparison group. Under a no-anticipation assumption, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time-series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment, provided that the model used for the extrapolation is correctly specified. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for possibly high-dimensional covariates by machine learning. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ consistent behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors under specific regularity conditions. We apply the framework to the compulsory licensing of enemy-owned patents in the United States in 1919. Licensing raised patenting in the licensed subclasses and in technologically close ones alike, so that a comparison-group design understates the total effect.
item.dc:creator: Martin Huber

item.title: Sharp Fr\'echet--Hoeffding Bounds under Selectively Incomplete Observation
item.description: arXiv:2611.03075v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Incomplete records can sharpen bounds on joint outcome probabilities even when no pair of outcomes is jointly observed. I derive sharp pointwise Fr\'echet--Hoeffding bounds combining known population marginals with selectively observed records, without restricting the observation mechanism. I establish an exact reduction of the identification problem to finite-dimensional optimization, yielding computable characterizations of both bounds. Illustrations involving income mobility, potential outcomes, and split questionnaires demonstrate how incomplete records can improve identification relative to the classical bounds.
item.dc:creator: Rami V. Tabri

item.title: Double Machine Learning for Panel Data: Identification, Specification, and a Bank Regulation Effect
item.description: arXiv:2611.07249v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper examines robustness and causal interpretation of panel estimates using double/debiased machine learning. The prototype treatment setup is the 2018 US banking regulation. Under common treatment timing, we characterize identification and nuisance restrictions and derive exact bank-level representations of specified "within" and "first-difference" scores. Simulations assess panel model transformation-induced specification bias and inference under weaker overlap. Empirically, estimates vary with asset-size classification and prior growth. Prior-growth adjustment reduces overlap-weighted estimates across four Machine Learners (ML); doubly robust estimates depend on the fitted propensity and concentrated weights. Both bank groups received relief, so we estimate differential exposure effects. The findings highlight specification issues and the relation between functional-form robustness and causal identification.
item.dc:creator: Ali Habibnia, Esfandiar Maasoumi, Gaurav Shah

item.title: Do Modern Difference-in-Differences Estimators Change Published Findings in Business Research?
item.description: arXiv:2611.11003v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Staggered-adoption difference-in-differences (DiD) designs are a workhorse of empirical research in business-school journals. The two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimator that typically implements them can place negative weights on heterogeneous treatment effects. We ask whether negative weights change published findings by reanalyzing staggered-adoption specifications in business-school journals with journal-wide public replication archives. Following Hull (2026), we use large language model agents to identify eligible specifications, replicate the published TWFE estimate, and re-estimate each specification with the DiD-averaging estimator of Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) and the imputation estimator of Borusyak et al. (2024). We re-estimate 355 specifications from 40 papers. Across the 283 DiD-averaging and 306 imputation comparisons that pass Hull's leverage screen, from 28 and 29 papers, TWFE and modern estimates have correlations of 0.61 and 0.70, change sign in 25.1 and 18.0 percent of comparisons, and differ significantly with opposite signs in 10.2 and 7.2 percent. Modern standard errors are 1.61 and 1.30 times those of TWFE. Including the comparisons that fail the screen leaves these figures essentially unchanged. Our results suggest that TWFE and heterogeneity-robust estimators disagree in a non-negligible share of the published staggered designs we re-estimate, and more often than in economics.
item.dc:creator: Davide Proserpio

item.title: Hedging out the HEDGE Bias: Identifying Dynamic Partial-Equilibrium Effects with Panel LP-IV
item.description: arXiv:2611.14434v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cross-sectional designs are widely used to estimate dynamic partial-equilibrium effects of an aggregate treatment. We show analytically that these estimates are biased when exposures to the treatment and to aggregate confounders are correlated or the confounders feed back into the treatment. This paper develops the heterogeneous-exposure local-projection instrumental variables (HELP-IV) framework, which compares units while holding the confounder path fixed by instrumenting the treatment and this path with exposure-weighted shock proxies. We prove that HELP-IV identifies the partial-equilibrium effect. We further extend the framework, with the corresponding inference, to multiple exposure margins and confounders, forward-looking outcomes, and cumulative multipliers. Finally, we apply HELP-IV to state fiscal multipliers and regional stock-wealth effects, where it yields partial-equilibrium effects that are smaller than conventional estimates and deliver different implications when ported to macroeconomic models.
item.dc:creator: Endong Wang, Ren Zhang

item.title: On the modelling and prediction of high-dimensional functional time series
item.description: arXiv:2406.00700v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a two-step procedure to model and predict high-dimensional functional time series, where the number of function-valued time series $p$ is large in relation to the length of time series $n$. Our first step performs an eigenanalysis of a positive definite matrix, which leads to a one-to-one linear transformation for the original high-dimensional functional time series, and the transformed curve series can be segmented into several groups such that any two subseries from any two different groups are uncorrelated both contemporaneously and serially. Consequently in our second step those groups are handled separately without the information loss on the overall linear dynamic structure. The second step is devoted to establishing a finite-dimensional dynamical structure for all the transformed functional time series within each group. Furthermore the finite-dimensional structure is represented by that of a vector time series. Modelling and forecasting for the original high-dimensional functional time series are realized via those for the vector time series in all the groups. We investigate the theoretical properties of our proposed methods, and illustrate the finite-sample performance through both extensive simulation and two real datasets.
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Chang, Qin Fang, Xinghao Qiao, Qiwei Yao

item.title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Just Classification and a Few Regressions
item.description: arXiv:2509.21172v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to recover a reward function from observed behavior, but rewards are typically only partially identified: many reward--value pairs can induce the same behavior policy. We study this problem in the maximum-entropy, or Gumbel-shock, model under a broad class of statewise affine normalization constraints, with anchor-action constraints as a special case. This leads to Generalized Policy-to-$Q$-to-Reward (GenPQR), a modular approach to normalized reward recovery based on policy estimation and $Q$-evaluation via the Bellman equation; both components can be instantiated with off-the-shelf classification and regression methods. We establish modular finite-sample guarantees under general function approximation, with separate terms for policy-estimation and $Q$-function estimation error. We also give explicit bounds for GenPQR with fitted $Q$-evaluation. In experiments, GenPQR improves on DeepPQR in reward recovery. Our guarantees extend beyond anchor actions, accommodate large action spaces, and are not tied to a specific neural-network architecture or training procedure.
item.dc:creator: Lars van der Laan, Nathan Kallus, Aurelien Bibaut

item.title: Balancing Weights for Causal Mediation Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2512.09337v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Causal mediation analysis decomposes the average treatment effect into components that operate through intermediate variables and a component that does not. This paper studies weighting estimation of generalized mediation functionals, whose contrasts include natural direct and indirect effects, for any fixed finite number of causally ordered mediators. Inverse propensity score weights are vulnerable to (a) weight instability, because they are products of estimated probability ratios, and (b) finite-sample covariate and mediator imbalance, which can bias the estimator. We instead propose sequential balancing weights, which address (a) by minimizing weight dispersion and (b) by imposing exact balance. Stage one balances covariates between a treatment group and the full sample. Each later stage adds the next mediator and balances a treatment group against the preceding weighted group. A finite-sample bias decomposition of the augmented weighting estimator determines these variables and targets. When exact balance cannot be attained in a small sample, the procedure relaxes the balancing conditions by tolerances selected without using the outcome. Under the stated assumptions, the estimated weights converge at every stage to their population inverse-probability counterparts, with errors from preceding stages entering additively. We also establish asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency of the augmented weighting estimator, together with conditions for consistent variance estimation. In the main simulation design with two ordered mediators, the proposed weights outperform the compared methods in bias, root mean squared error, and coverage. In a small media-framing experiment with two ordered mediators, the proposed weights reduce the imbalance left by propensity-score weighting.
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Kawato

item.title: Calibeating Prediction-Powered Inference
item.description: arXiv:2604.21260v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study semisupervised mean estimation with a small labeled sample, a large unlabeled sample, and a black-box prediction model whose output may be miscalibrated. A standard approach in this setting is augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) [Robins et al., 1994], which protects against prediction-model misspecification but may be inefficient when the prediction score is poorly aligned with the outcome scale. We introduce Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference, which post-hoc calibrates the prediction score on the labeled sample before using it for semisupervised estimation. This simple step requires no retraining and can calibeat the original score, improving it both as a predictor of the outcome and as a regression adjustment for semisupervised inference. We study both linear and isotonic calibration. For isotonic calibration, we establish first-order optimality guarantees: isotonic post-processing can improve predictive accuracy and estimator efficiency relative to the original score and simpler post-processing rules, while replacing the fitted isotonic score by its conditional-mean oracle yields no additional first-order variance reduction. For linear calibration, we show first-order equivalence to PPI++. We also clarify the relationship between existing estimators, showing that the original PPI estimator is a special case of AIPW and can be inefficient when the prediction model is accurate, while PPI++ is AIPW with empirical efficiency maximization [Rubin and van der Laan, 2008]. In simulations and real-data experiments, our calibrated estimators often outperform PPI and are competitive with, or outperform, AIPW and PPI++. We provide an accompanying Python package, ppi_aipw, at https://larsvanderlaan.github.io/ppi-aipw/.
item.dc:creator: Lars van der Laan, Mark Van Der Laan

item.title: Ramping Procurement and Bid-Cost Recovery in Real-Time Market
item.description: arXiv:2606.19599v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study ramping procurement co-optimized with economic dispatch under net-demand uncertainty. We examine two flexible ramp product designs implemented by grid operators: single-interval and multi-interval co-optimization. Both rely on rolling-window stochastic optimization with binding and advisory interval decisions. We develop analytical frameworks to evaluate generator profits, consumer payments, bid cost recovery (BCR), and operational efficiency. In particular, net-demand uncertainty may lead to generator under-compensation, requiring discriminatory BCR. While operational efficiency is invariant to energy and ramp prices, producer profits and consumer payments depend critically on pricing. We examine locational marginal pricing (LMP) and two uniform pricing: maximum dispatch cost pricing (MDCP) and maximum temporal locational marginal pricing (MTLMP). With out-of-market BCR, LMP yields discriminatory energy prices, whereas MDCP eliminates BCR and MTLMP does so in most cases. This property enables us to establish truthful bidding incentives for price-taking generators under MDCP. Our analysis highlights trade-offs between single- and multi-interval co-optimization and pricing designs: multi-interval energy-ramp co-optimization outperforms single-interval co-optimization when ramping forecasts are accurate and ramping needs are tight, but its advantage diminishes under large forecast errors and moderate ramping needs. Empirical results on CAISO and ERCOT data show that MDCP and MTLMP increase producer profits with negligible BCR, albeit at the expense of higher consumer payments relative to LMP.
item.dc:creator: Cong Chen, Valentina Norambuena, Lang Tong

item.title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Bellman Tournaments
item.description: arXiv:2610.35748v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Model selection and hyperparameter tuning pose a central challenge in off-policy evaluation (OPE) because estimation errors in fitted $Q$-functions and occupancy ratios cannot be directly evaluated using held-out transition data. Existing Bellman-residual-based validation methods often require auxiliary regressions, while many minimax-based methods require optimization over separate critic classes. We propose pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a family of penalized Bellman tournament methods that reduces validation to computing held-out sample averages. PBV constructs critics from pairwise candidate differences, on the log scale for occupancy ratios, and selects the candidate with the smallest worst-case penalized score. This construction approximates oracle critics given by $Q$-function errors and log ratios of candidate to true occupancy ratios, whose Bellman and adjoint Bellman moments control estimation error. Critic penalties account for approximation error under candidate-class misspecification. We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification. For $Q$-function selection, unweighted PBV avoids importance weighting but requires a coercivity condition on a quadratic form induced by the Bellman operator. Importance-weighted PBV (IW-PBV) uses marginalized importance weighting to exploit Bellman contraction under the target-policy occupancy measure, avoiding this condition. For occupancy-ratio selection, adjoint PBV (A-PBV) exploits KL contraction of the adjoint Bellman operator to obtain oracle guarantees under the offline data law. On Hopper and DeepOPE, unweighted PBV is competitive with LSTD-Tournament, often achieving higher accuracy on Hopper, while importance weighting can further improve performance under controlled overlap.
item.dc:creator: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus

item.title: When Listwise Deletion Works: Causal Diagrams and Complete-Case Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.04366v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Listwise deletion (LWD) appears more common than imputation: at least 50% of the observational causal studies we review in leading journals state or imply it, while 7% describe an imputation model. We develop a framework for when complete-case regression consistently estimates the population average treatment effect (ATE). With a constant unit-level treatment effect, two checks suffice: whether covariates and the missingness indicator satisfy the adjustment criterion in an augmented causal diagram (DAG), and whether the estimator pools within-covariate comparisons appropriately, possibly using inverse propensity weighting. A collider--mediator illustration highlights the first check: the same missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism can require different adjustment choices. With heterogeneous effects, conditional effects must be transportable to the population and be reweighted to its population distribution. These formal results provide practical checks for applied researchers to run complete case regressions, recover existing guidance as special cases, and are illustrated with applications across fields.
item.dc:creator: Wenxin Lin, Shiyao Liu
